title: Complex Numbers
tagline: The need for complex numbers, i and its powers, algebraic operations, conjugate, modulus, Argand plane, cube roots of unity.

sourceNote.boardprep: Original study material written by BoardPrep for the CISCE ISC Class XI Mathematics syllabus (official-verified baseline, examination year 2027). Syllabus unit and chapter title were taken from the official-verified ISC Mathematics registry entry; no board examination paper was consulted, so every question is original practice and not a previous year question.

overview.intro: Some equations have no real solutions. For example, x^2 = -1 has no real number solution because no real number squared gives a negative number. To deal with this, mathematicians introduced a new kind of number, the complex number. The basic unit is i, defined by i^2 = -1. A complex number is written as a + ib, where a and b are real numbers. This chapter develops the algebra of complex numbers, their geometric picture on the Argand plane, and a few important results such as the cube roots of unity.

facts.label: Core ideas
facts.value: i = sqrt(-1); integral powers of i; a + ib form; addition, subtraction, multiplication and division; conjugate; modulus; Argand plane; cube roots of unity and their properties

learningOutcomes: State the definition of i and its integral powers.
Express a complex number in the form a + ib.
Add, subtract, multiply and divide complex numbers.
Find the conjugate and modulus of a complex number and use their basic properties.
Identify real and imaginary parts and locate a complex number on the Argand plane.
Use the basic properties of the cube roots of unity.

blocks.text: Real numbers are enough for many equations, but not for all of them. The equation x^2 + 1 = 0 has no real solution, because the square of any real number is non-negative. To solve such equations, we define a new number i with the property i^2 = -1. Once this is done, every quadratic equation has a solution in the complex number system. This is one reason complex numbers are not just an artificial extension; they complete the number system for polynomial equations.

items: i is defined by i^2 = -1.
A complex number has the form a + ib with a, b real.
Real numbers are a special case with b = 0.
Complex numbers let every quadratic equation have a solution.

items.text: The equation x^2 + 1 = 0 has solutions i and -i, which are not real but are complex.
items.note: The point is not that i is 'imaginary' in the everyday sense; it is a number that extends the system so that equations like this can be solved.

blocks.text: Complex numbers are added and subtracted by treating i like a variable, but remembering that i^2 = -1. To multiply, expand as usual and then replace i^2 by -1. To divide, multiply numerator and denominator by the conjugate of the denominator so that the denominator becomes a real number. Once the denominator is real, the result can be written clearly in the form a + ib.

items: Addition and subtraction are done by combining real parts and imaginary parts separately.
Multiplication expands like ordinary algebra and uses i^2 = -1.
Division uses the conjugate of the denominator.
The result of any arithmetic operation can be written as a + ib with a, b real.

items.text: If z1 = 2 + 3i and z2 = 1 + i, then z1 + z2 = 3 + 4i and z1 - z2 = 1 + 2i. For multiplication, (2 + 3i)(1 + i) = 2 + 2i + 3i + 3i^2 = 2 + 5i - 3 = -1 + 5i.
items.note: The key step in multiplication is that i^2 becomes -1, which changes the final real part.

blocks.text: For a complex number z = a + ib, the conjugate is a - ib. Conjugation changes the sign of the imaginary part only. It is useful because z times its conjugate gives a^2 + b^2, which is a real number. The modulus of z is the distance from the origin to the point (a, b) in the Argand plane, and its square is exactly a^2 + b^2. These ideas connect algebra with geometry.

items: The conjugate of a + ib is a - ib.
Conjugation changes only the sign of the imaginary part.
z times conjugate z equals |z|^2.
The modulus is sqrt(a^2 + b^2).
The modulus is the distance from the origin in the Argand plane.

items.text: For z = 2 - 3i, the conjugate is 2 + 3i and the modulus is sqrt(2^2 + (-3)^2) = sqrt13. Then z times its conjugate is 13, confirming |z|^2 = a^2 + b^2.
items.note: This example shows both the algebraic and geometric meanings of modulus and conjugate.

blocks.text: A complex number a + ib can be represented as the point (a, b) in a plane called the Argand plane. The horizontal axis usually represents the real part, and the vertical axis represents the imaginary part. This picture is more than a convenience; it turns operations on complex numbers into geometric ideas. Addition becomes vector addition, and the modulus becomes the length of the position vector.

items: The Argand plane has a real axis and an imaginary axis.
a + ib is plotted as (a, b).
The modulus is the distance from (0, 0) to (a, b).
Geometry helps explain addition and the meaning of conjugate.

items.text: The complex number 2 + 3i corresponds to the point (2, 3), and its conjugate 2 - 3i is the reflection of that point across the real axis.
items.note: The reflection picture is one reason conjugation is so useful; it reverses the sign of the imaginary coordinate only.

blocks.text: The cube roots of unity are the numbers whose cube is 1. The obvious one is 1, but there are two others, which are complex. They satisfy 1 + omega + omega^2 = 0 and omega^3 = 1. These properties are useful in simplifying expressions involving these numbers and in solving certain equations. They also give a neat example of how complex numbers are not just a fix for one equation but a structure with their own identities.

items: The cube roots of unity are 1, omega and omega^2.
omega^3 = 1.
1 + omega + omega^2 = 0.
omega^2 is the conjugate of omega.
These rules help simplify expressions that contain omega.

items.text: If an expression contains omega + omega^2, it can be replaced by -1, because 1 + omega + omega^2 = 0 implies omega + omega^2 = -1.
items.note: The cube roots of unity are a small but rich set of examples that show how complex numbers behave in a closed system.

figures.caption: Figure: Argand plane for a complex number and its conjugate
figures.description: A point a + ib and its reflection a - ib across the real axis, with the modulus shown as the distance from the origin.

keyPoints: A complex number is written a + ib with a, b real.
Addition and multiplication use ordinary algebra with i^2 = -1.
Division is done by multiplying numerator and denominator by the conjugate of the denominator.
The conjugate of a + ib is a - ib.
The modulus is sqrt(a^2 + b^2) and equals the distance from the origin in the Argand plane.
The cube roots of unity satisfy omega^3 = 1 and 1 + omega + omega^2 = 0.
examFocus: When dividing, always rationalise the denominator by multiplying by the conjugate; leaving i in the denominator is usually not the final form.
When finding modulus, do not forget the square root; a^2 + b^2 is |z|^2, not |z|.

vocabulary.meaning: A number of the form a + ib where a and b are real and i^2 = -1.
The number a - ib for z = a + ib.
The distance from the origin to a + ib, equal to sqrt(a^2 + b^2).
A plane in which a complex number a + ib is represented by the point (a, b).

options: sqrt(-1) only as a symbol with no value
questions.explanation: The symbol i is defined so that i^2 = -1.
questions.commonMistake: Thinking i^2 = 1 because of forgetting the negative.

questions.explanation: Conjugation changes the sign of the imaginary part only.
questions.commonMistake: Negating the real part as well, or leaving the sign unchanged.

questions.explanation: The modulus is sqrt(2^2 + (-3)^2) = sqrt(4 + 9) = sqrt13.
questions.commonMistake: Forgetting the square root, or squaring -3 incorrectly as -9.

questions.prompt: Simplify (2 + i)(3 - i) and write it in the form a + ib.
questions.commonMistake: Forgetting that -i^2 becomes +1, or combining the real and imaginary parts incorrectly.

questions.prompt: If omega is a complex cube root of unity, simplify omega^2 + omega + 1 and omega^4 + omega.
questions.answer: omega^2 + omega + 1 = 0 because the cube roots of unity satisfy 1 + omega + omega^2 = 0. omega^4 + omega = omega + omega = 2 omega, because omega^4 = omega^3 * omega = 1 * omega = omega.
questions.explanation: The simplification uses the defining properties of the cube roots of unity.
questions.commonMistake: Forgetting omega^3 = 1 when reducing omega^4, or not recognising that the sum of all three cube roots is 0.
